playbook:
- Claims must match the private result, so I always file exactly what the office tells me. Lying on a claim is not an option, and I should not waste reasoning on it. When I hit, I claim hit; when I miss, I claim miss.
- I follow the standing fire order (fire at the next station round the picket) every round. Deviating gets me nothing unless I have a specific read on a hidden cell.
- I never fire on Harbor. The +3 payroll grab is tempting but the threatened retaliation (being put off the board) costs far more over the remaining rounds.
- Hiding: shots are blind guesses and in this episode every single shot all game was a miss, so cell choice barely matters. Still, I avoid the obvious center (4-6), avoid repeating my last cell, and vary between low (1-3) and high (7-9). I never announce my real cell or pattern in notes.
- Escort claims are the dominant scoring lever: a mutual pair pays +5 each per round, dwarfing the 4/−1 swing of a hit. Securing one is my first priority from round 1.
- Naming an escort costs me nothing even if unreciprocated — the only failure mode is no payout. This episode I filed [salvage: none] in round 6 after proposing a deal; that was strictly worse than naming Gamma. I never file "none" unless I have a specific reason to deny someone a payout; I always name my proposed partner.
- Consistency is everything: if I propose "Echo escorts Gamma" in a note, I must actually file [salvage: Gamma] every round, including the last, so the partner sees reliable reciprocity. This episode my round-6 defection to "none" contradicted my own note and guaranteed nothing could pay out.
- When a partner doesn't reciprocate after 2-3 rounds, I check who (if anyone) named me and switch to naming them, and I use my next note to propose that new pairing explicitly. If the other boats only post filler like "steady on station" and never coordinate, I still name one boat every round — it costs nothing and leaves the door open if they ever come around.
- I pair escorting with a boat that is not my standing-order target, so a hit from me doesn't sour the deal — ideally the boat that fires on me, since I never shoot them and can even advertise that.
- Notes are my only coordination channel. I keep them short, public, and explicit: name the partner, state the mutual deal, commit to it. I propose in round 1 and reinforce in later notes rather than repeating the same unrewarded proposal forever.
- Shooting income is mostly luck; over 6 rounds all nine shots missed and everyone finished at 0. I keep firing on order for the small chance of +4, but I treat the escort deal and never firing on Harbor as the parts of the game I actually control.

1.text:
When the escort stage comes, I always name the boat most likely to name me back, and I use my station note earlier that round to signal the pairing — a mutual escort pays 5 points to each of us, far more than any single hit, and naming someone costs nothing even if it fails.

When proposing an escort, I watch whether the other boat actually echoes the proposal in its own note or names me in salvage; if after two rounds they haven't reciprocated, they are not locking in the pairing — I switch my signal and my salvage claim to whoever's notes show any engagement, rather than repeating "escort me, Echo" at a wall all six rounds.

When other boats only post filler like "steady on station," I don't give up on coordination but I raise the stakes in my note: name the exact claim I'll file ("Foxtrot will salvage Echo"), because vague offers are easier to ignore than explicit commitments.

When posting notes, I make them do work: propose an escort partner or report read patterns from the log, instead of filler like "steady on station."

When choosing a hide cell, I never settle into one or two cells across the game even while dodging successfully — six rounds of misses don't mean my pattern is safe, they mean I've been lucky, and cycling 3/5/3/5 is exactly the kind of rhythm an observant shooter will eventually test.

When choosing a hide cell, I pick based on where my assigned shooter has been firing and rotate through cells they have never shot at all; I treat cells untouched in the log as safer than cells they recently missed, because a shooter who misses twice in one spot may return there.

When firing, I read the target's hide history in the log rather than repeating one cell — I fired 5 at Gamma repeatedly with no info it would land; with nine unknown cells, spreading shots across the board is at least informative and no worse, and if the log ever reveals a target's habit I hammer it.

When firing, if a cell has repeatedly missed and there's no log evidence about the target's position, I move on rather than firing the same cell a third time.

When deciding whether to fire on Harbor, I do not: the 3-point transfer is not worth being put off the board, and Harbor's note explicitly promises retaliation.

When filing a claim, I tell the truth always; results are visible in the round summary anyway, and lying only risks credibility with potential escort partners for zero gain.

When I'm being repeatedly targeted by the same boat, I read the log for their firing pattern rather than guessing, and I move to a cell outside that pattern even if it feels less natural.

When the game is near its end and I'm behind or tied, I prioritize the guaranteed escort payout over hoping for a hit — 5 certain points beats a 1-in-9 shot at 4 — and I say so plainly in my note as a final-round offer.

When everyone is at 0 late in the game, I treat the whole pool as desperate for the escort payday and expect cooperation proposals to be taken more seriously, so my late-round note offers are more likely to land than my round-1 ones — but I still need to verify the pairing happened before assuming it will repeat.

2.text:
When deciding where to hide, I track which cells my designated shooter has fired at recently and avoid those, plus avoid repeating my last hiding cell if it was just hit — the 4 to 5 point swing from a fresh hit on me matters more than variety for its own sake. I vary among edge and off-center cells rather than settling into a pattern, since I'm the fixed target of one specific boat every round.

When firing, I always shoot my standing-order target rather than improvising, but I never fire the same cell twice at a target that keeps missing — I rotate through plausible cells (center, then cells the target has favored or recently vacated) because a stationary firing pattern got me six straight misses. I never fire on Harbor — 3 points is not worth being put off the board for the rest of the patrol.

When my shot result is told to me privately, I claim it truthfully every round, including the last. A false hit claim gains nothing real; the honest claim is always right.

When the escort claim comes up, my first rule is: NAME ONLY BOATS THAT ACTUALLY EXIST IN THIS PATROL. I threw away every escort bonus by naming "Beta", a boat not on the roster — an invalid claim pays nothing no matter what my partner does. I name one of the listed live boats (Echo, Foxtrot, Harbor as the roster gives), never "none" unless coordination clearly failed.

On escort coordination itself: mutual escort is 5 points each — more than a hit — so I propose a pairing in round one with the boat that shoots me. But I verify the deal is real before relying on it: a partner that replies only "steady on station" and never names me back has not agreed. If round one's results show no reciprocation, I switch my note to an explicit fresh proposal naming the exact pairing ("I will name Foxtrot; Foxtrot name Gamma") and try the other boat rather than repeating a failed one-sided claim into the last round.

When posting notes, I use them as my only coordination channel: I state my escort proposal plainly, then signal consistency, and I actively read others' notes for counter-proposals instead of treating "steady on station" as acceptance. A one-line note is cheap; I use it to confirm the reciprocal plan each time something changes.

When scoring the endgame, I remember the biggest lever is a VALID, reciprocated escort loop, the second is landing standing-order shots (which requires rotating my aim), and only then avoiding hits. Zero after six rounds means the coordination failed — next time I check the roster, check the reciprocation, and fix it by round two rather than discovering at the end that my claims were invalid all along.
